newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Horn urges EU to take new members on merit.
newsitem.headline: Horn urges EU to take new members on merit.

text.p: Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn appealed to the European Union (EU) on Monday not to open simultaneous talks with all countries applying for membership but to start with those most ready to join.

Addressing a ceremony to mark the fifth anniversary of Hungary signing an association agreement with the EU, Horn said he was concerned that member states were assuming talks would begin with all applicants.

"I would like a different approach," he said. "Country reports to be submitted in the autumn of 1997 will outline the preparedness and development of each country for EU membership -- these should be the criteria for opening talks.
"I am convinced that on that basis Hungary would be in the first group," he added.

Horn was speaking on his return from an EU summit in Dublin which paved the way for intense negotiations over the next six months to draw up a new EU treaty in time for an influx of new members, mainly from ex-communist East Europe.
Aspiring members were told talks would begin in 1998 with eventual membership envisaged soon after the turn of the century.

Horn stressed that while other applicant countries such as Poland and Slovakia may have better growth figures, the strength and depth of Hungary's restructuring put it at the top of the pile for meeting EU membership criteria.

"In terms of reform of public sector financing, the extent of privatisation and the scope of the private sector in the economy, and macroeconomic indicators, no other country can claim to have come so far," he said.
Horn also appealed to Brussels to change the method of calculating the cost to the EU of embracing new members.
He said current forecasts painted a falsely pessimistic picture and should take into account trade surpluses member countries are already accumulating with countries such as Hungary.
"While certain (West European) countries and companies make major profits (in Central Europe) these do not appear to be reflected in the budget predictions of the EU," he said.
Hungary was the first former communist country to sign an association agreement with the EU, which allows certain trade concessions as well as access to development aid.
Horn asked the EU to set up a fund to help Hungary prepare for entry and suggested that the year 2000 was a realistic date for entry.
"I suggest two o'clock in the afternoon on December 24, 2000 -- just in time for the Christmas celebrations," he said.
